South Korea's headline inflation moderated last month but remained above the central bank's 2% target, underscoring the challenge of taming price pressures stoked by the energy shock and artificial-intelligence boom.

The result gives Bank of Korea policymakers another dataset to contemplate ahead of this month's meeting, as they weigh further tightening to counter inflation fanned by the Middle East conflict and AI-fueled demand.
South Korea's consumer-price index rose 2.9% in September from a year earlier, slowing from 3.1% in August, the Ministry of Data and Statistics said Friday.
The latest reading was exactly in line with the median forecast by 17 economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal.

It remains unclear whether the latest print will alter the BOK's calculus, with consensus pointing to further rate increases in the coming months but policymakers potentially pausing to assess the lagged effects of back-to-back hikes in July and August.

In September, agricultural-product price growth slowed, with sticky rice and apple prices falling 10% and 9.2%, respectively, from a year earlier in September, while fuel-price growth accelerated, with gasoline and diesel prices rising 12% and 20%, respectively.

South Korea's Inflation Eases But Stays Sticky — Update
By Kwanwoo Jun

South Korea's headline inflation moderated last month but remained above the central bank's 2% target, underscoring the challenge of taming price pressures stoked by the energy shock and artificial-intelligence boom.

The result gives Bank of Korea policymakers another dataset to contemplate ahead of this month's meeting, as they weigh further tightening to counter inflation fanned by the Middle East conflict and AI-fueled demand.
South Korea's consumer-price index rose 2.9% in September from a year earlier, slowing from 3.1% in August, the Ministry of Data and Statistics said Friday.
The latest reading was exactly in line with the median forecast by 17 economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal.

It remains unclear whether the latest print will alter the BOK's calculus, with consensus pointing to further rate increases in the coming months but policymakers potentially pausing to assess the lagged effects of back-to-back hikes in July and August.
The finance ministry said a government cap on fuel prices and increased supplies of agricultural products during the Chuseok holiday helped ease price pressures.
On a month-on-month basis, consumer prices rose 0.3% in September, compared with the poll's forecast for a 0.4% increase. They fell 0.2% in August.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.8% on year in September but edged down 0.1% on month.

In September, agricultural-product price growth slowed, with sticky rice and apple prices falling 10% and 9.2%, respectively, from a year earlier in September, while fuel-price growth accelerated, with gasoline and diesel prices rising 12% and 20%, respectively.

Policymakers remain mindful of elevated underlying inflation, which has stayed at or above the 2% target for about a year, as they watch for spillovers from the country's stronger-than-expected, chip-led economic growth into wages and consumer prices.

The BOK now expects the economy to grow 3.3% this year, up from its May forecast of 2.6%. It maintains its headline inflation forecast of 2.7% for 2026 but expects core inflation to average 2.5%, up from its previous projection of 2.4%.
Most analysts expect the BOK to deliver further rate increases in the coming months, with some forecasting that it could briefly pause in October following back-to-back hikes.

The probability of another rate increase at the Oct. 22 meeting "is not particularly high" as the BOK may now prefer a more gradual pace of tightening, JPMorgan economist Seok Gil Park said recently. Park said the BOK could deliver additional hikes in November this year and in February and May next year.
